verdicts.note: Sound. Plato 199d: 'I am not asking whether he is of some mother or father; the question would be ridiculous, whether Love is love of a mother or a father.' The first half uses the parentage sense of the genitive. Socrates uses the same construction at 203a when he asks who Love's father and mother are, so 'whose child Love is' is a reading Jowett's ambiguous 'the love of a father' allows. 'as though he were the love of some father or mother' keeps Jowett's words, and 'that would be a ridiculous question' renders τὸ ἐρώτημα. The father analogy and 'of something' are intact. 'does it always have an object?' unpacks 'such as to be of something' without answering it; 7.8-7.9 still ask and answer the either/or. 7.1-7.3 ('Very true'; 'the same of a mother?') still fit. No new defect.

Modernizing the syntax is right, and 'by his very nature' renders Jowett's 'essentially' (αὐτὸ τοῦθ᾽ ὅπερ ἔστιν). But the edit also changes 'something' to 'someone' at the middle step of the father / brother / Love analogy. Plato uses the same τινός in all three questions (199d-e), and Jowett has 'something' each time. The round-2 text keeps 'is a father the father of something?' (7.0) and 'Is Love of something, or of nothing?' (7.8). The word this argument turns on should be the same at every step. A person-word here also nudges the listener toward 'love of someone', whereas the argument abstracts the object of love (beauty, the good). Keep everything else and restore 'something'.
verdicts.proposed_replace: 'Let me ask you one more question to make my meaning clear: isn't a brother, by his very nature, the brother of something?'

verdicts.note: Sound and grounded in the Greek. Plato 200a: 'keep this to yourself, remembering what it is of' (φύλαξον παρὰ σαυτῷ μεμνημένος ὅτου); Jowett's 'Keep in mind' covers only the remembering. 'hold that answer back for now' tells the listener that the object of love is being kept in reserve; Socrates brings it back at 7.28-7.30 (beauty). 'tell me just this' renders τοσόνδε. 'does Love desire the thing he loves?' keeps Jowett's 'desires that of which love is', repeats 7.12's 'the thing he loves', and removes the 'love is love of' tongue-twister. 7.11 'Yes, surely' still fits. No added fact or argument.

Faithful: 'have ... or not' is Jowett's 'possess, or ... not possess'. 'have' is the elenchus's own word (7.20, 7.22, 7.24, 7.32, 7.34), and 7.13 'Probably not' still answers it (Plato 200a: 'not having it, probably').
Agathon's short reply. 'I'd say' is natural, has no voice problem, and echoes Socrates's 'I'd like you to consider' in 7.14. Meaning unchanged.
Faithful; 'someone who is' replaces archaic 'he who is' with no change of sense.
Faithful and clearer by ear. 'what we have already agreed' matches the chapter's recurring 'agreed' (7.32, 7.54, 7.55).

Sound. Jowett's 'want' here means lack: Plato 200b says the one who is these things 'would not be lacking' (ἐνδεής) in them. That applies the glossary and keeps the desire-implies-lack step; 7.19 'Very true' fits.

Faithful and far easier to follow aloud. 'kept for him in the future' = 'preserved to him'; 'does not yet exist for him, something he does not yet have' = 'non-existent to him ... as yet he has not got'. The lack rule that rests on it is intact, and 7.23 fits.

Removing 'just' (heard as 'merely') is right, but 'fair point' puts 'fair' in its 'just, reasonable' sense into the beauty elenchus, one sentence before 'Love is the love of beauty and not of ugliness'. The glossary says 'Never "fair" meaning just', and ties it to this argument. In chapter 7 Jowett's 'fair' always means beautiful, and Tinct readers can compare the original edition side by side. (The same sense of 'fair' at 3.2, 3.5 and 8.14 is harmless, far from the argument.) Plato 201a: 'and you speak rightly, my friend' (ἐπιεικῶς γε λέγεις). Use wording outside the fair/beautiful and good chains.
verdicts.proposed_replace: 'Yes, my friend, and you were right to say so.

verdicts.note: Sound, and it answers the brief's question. Plato 201b ('has it not been agreed that [one] loves what [one] lacks and does not have?') has no expressed subject, so impersonal 'one' is faithful and no stronger than Plato. Unlike 'a man', 'one' can include Love, so 7.34 'Then Love lacks beauty' follows as it does in Plato. The step from lover to Love is Plato's own, not added. 'lacks and does not have' is the pair repeated at 7.34 and 7.36; lowercase 'love' states the general principle, and 7.33 'True' fits. Follow-up: 7.26, the agreement this recalls, still says 'a man' (see paragraph_problems).

Right: Agathon's thesis was that the god Love is beautiful, and 7.34 capitalizes the same subject (ὁ Ἔρως). The change is visible on the page only; nothing changes for a listener. See paragraph_problems for 7.42.

Faithful: Plato 201c asks whether good things are also beautiful (τἀγαθὰ ... καλά, plural and generic), so 'what is good' is exact. 7.41 'Yes' and the 7.42 inference (lacking the beautiful, love lacks the good) still follow.
Diotima speaks without contractions, and 'Do you not see' is Jowett's own wording.
Correct speaker: Diotima asks this. The tag resolves the untagged turn in the nested dialogue.
Needed after R2-115. The paragraph now has 16 double quotes, all balanced, and Socrates's single quote stays open for the continuing speech, as the convention requires.
Correct speaker (Diotima). 'By everyone' remains Socrates's reply, and the quotes are balanced.

Acceptable, not an omission of substance. '(daimon)' is Jowett's parenthetical transliteration, a translator's note, like the cross-references '(compare 1 Alcibiades)', '(compare Gorgias)' and '(supra)' already dropped from 7.45. The content is kept in full: a great spirit, midway between the divine and the mortal, one of many in-between powers. 'spirit' is Jowett's own word, echoed by 'spirits', 'spiritual' and 7.49's 'the spirit Love'. Aloud, 'daimon' is heard as 'demon', which would invert the meaning.

Sound, and verified in the Greek. Plato 203a: θεὸς δὲ ἀνθρώπῳ οὐ μείγνυται ... θεοῖς πρὸς ἀνθρώπους, that is, 'a god (singular, no article) does not mix with a human being; all dealings and conversation of gods with humans are through this'. The AFTER follows that singular-then-plural shape exactly, and Jowett's own paragraph says 'between gods and men'. It removes a monotheistic reading without importing anything. The plural 'men are' fits, and the glossary's 'communication' is applied.

Accurate unpacking of names. The Greek word poros means way, means, resource, and Jowett himself says Love is 'fertile in resources' like his father (7.48, now 'full of resources'). 'Resource' explains that inheritance; Plato's wordplay continues at 203e, where Love is never 'resourceless' (ἀπορεῖ). Jowett's 'Plenty' is kept and reused as the name in 7.48. Metis means cunning intelligence or wisdom, which fits the scheming traits of the father's side in 7.48. 'Discretion' (now heard as tact) is replaced, not lost. The semicolon gives two breaths; the listener still hears five terms, but each is framed.

Fine. It is the standard sense of 'sophist' and matches 7.58 ('one of those professional teachers of wisdom'), close to 1.46 ('professional teachers'). 'clever' keeps the edge of δεινός beside 'enchanter, a sorcerer'. The paragraph's pairing of philosopher (lover of wisdom) with sophist (professional teacher of wisdom) is Plato's own. The gloss now recurs almost verbatim ten paragraphs later in the same speech; that is harmless.

The right fix for a real contradiction with 7.48's 'always in need'. Plato 203e: Love is never resourceless (ἀπορεῖ) and never rich, and 'destitute' fits Jowett's want/wealth frame. It agrees with 'always poor ... always in need' (poor, but not destitute). It also avoids 'lack', which the argument reserves for what Love lacks (7.46, 7.49 'what he does not feel he lacks').

Faithful: Plato 204d says 'if someone asked us: "Socrates and Diotima, ...?"' (ἡμᾶς), so 'ask us both' is exact. It removes the vocative confusion. Single quotes nested inside Diotima's double quotes follow the pattern of 'good' and 'making' nearby, and are balanced.
Faithful: the natural order of Jowett's 'I have no answer ready' (Plato 204d: 'I could not answer that readily').

Sound. Plato asks the two questions in the same words ('the lover loves the beautiful/good things: what does he love?', 204d-e). The AFTER now repeats the beauty question with only 'good' substituted, which is exactly what Diotima says she is doing ('put the word "good" in place of the beautiful, and ask the question once more'). 'desire' is Jowett's own verb for the first question, and 'The possession of the good' still answers it. The 'loves loves' stumble is gone.

Sound. Plato 205b: 'if indeed all love the same things and always, why do we say that some love and others do not?' 'For you say' renders εἴπερ ('since indeed') at least as well as Jowett's 'whereas'; the logic is unchanged. 'in love' names the narrow everyday sense that the poetry analogy then explains, and 7.52 resumes it with 'said to love, or to be lovers'. 'I wonder about that myself' still fits.

Accurate gloss. Plato (205d) leaves the 'one form' unnamed, but here it is contrasted with money-making, athletics and philosophy, and followed by lovers seeking their other half. It is love directed at a person, so the gloss names what the context implies and adds no argument.

Sound. Plato 205e: 'if their own parts seem to them to be bad' (ἐὰν αὐτοῖς δοκῇ τὰ ἑαυτῶν πονηρὰ εἶναι). The Greek supplies both the referent (the limbs) and 'think', so no other translation is involved. 'bad' is kept for the good/bad chain, and the next sentence (about what people 'call' good) fits the judgment framing. The argument is unchanged.

Excellent and grounded in the Greek. Plato 206b: 'what you are saying needs divination' (μαντείας ... δεῖται), which fits within Jowett's 'the oracle requires an explanation'. 'prophet' matches 7.47's 'the arts of the prophet' and keeps Socrates's irony, and 'I will make my meaning clearer' still answers it.

Accurate and helpful. Plato 206c: 'all human beings are pregnant (κυοῦσιν), in body and in soul'. The gloss says only what pregnancy means, and anticipates 7.54 ('full to bursting') and 7.60 ('gives birth to what he conceived long ago') without adding to them. The pregnancy image is kept. The dashes read as an aside, and 'in body and in soul' still attaches to 'pregnant'.

Accurate. Plato 206d names Moira (Fate or destiny) and Eileithyia (the goddess of childbirth). Jowett fuses them ('the destiny or goddess of parturition'), and so does the AFTER, in words a listener understands.

Sound, and verified in Burnet's text at 206e: 'πάνυ μὲν οὖν, ἔφη. τί δὴ οὖν τῆς γεννήσεως; ὅτι ἀειγενές...'. The question and its answer sit in one speech of Diotima's. In Jowett the question is an untagged quote; only his later 'she replied' hints at Socrates, so the Greek chooses between readings Jowett allows. The question, the answer and the logic are unchanged, and asking and answering her own question suits Diotima's oracular voice. The spelled-out 'is love the love of reproduction' also matches the preceding 'The love of reproduction'.

Idiomatic, and 'also' (καί) is kept. But the edit leaves the premise in the same sentence group ('love is of the everlasting possession of the good') and 7.55 ('love is of the immortal') in the old formula; see paragraph_problems.
Diotima speaks without contractions; Jowett has 'See you not'.
Faithful to Jowett's 'even to the uttermost', and it removes the 'to the death ... to die' doubling. Nothing is lost.

Sound. Plato 208a: 'each single one of the knowledges undergoes the same thing' (μία ἑκάστη τῶν ἐπιστημῶν). 'piece of knowledge' fixes the unclear referent and fits the forgetting-and-renewal explanation that follows.

Accurate and useful. The gloss defines Jowett's word in its everyday sense, which blocks the doctrine-of-recollection misreading. Plato's word here is μελετᾶν, rehearsing, which 'implants a new memory in place of the departing one'. The gloss also makes the inference visible: calling something back implies that it had gone. No argument is added.

Faithful. Plato 208b ends 'ἀθάνατον δὲ ἄλλῃ' ('but the immortal, in another way'), the reading Jowett follows, with the verb left out. 'what is immortal is immortal in another way' supplies the natural sense, contrasting with the mortal 'sharing in immortality' by replacement. The preceding sentence ('The divine ... is always the same') explains the other way. It no longer says an immortal thing 'shares in' immortality.
Accurate: Codrus is a legendary king of Athens (tradition makes him the last of its kings), so 'an early king' is right, while 'the early king' implied the first or only one.

Faithful: Plato 208d says all men do all things for immortal virtue and fame, and the better they are, the more so. The comparative is kept ('the more they do so'), the universal claim is unchanged, and it is much easier to follow aloud.

Sound. Plato 209b: he 'desires to bring forth and to beget'. The edit restores Jowett's 'desires' and applies the glossary pair, keeping the chain 'reproduction / give birth' (7.53-7.55, 7.60, 7.63, 7.66).

Fine. 'carry' is the modern pregnancy sense of Jowett's 'contain', and 'fitting' renders προσήκει. Plato's pair at 209a is 'both to conceive and to bring forth' (καὶ κυῆσαι καὶ τεκεῖν), so 'and' is right; 'carry' stays within Jowett and the pregnancy image.
Sound. Plato 209b uses the same verb as 7.59 ('in the ugly he will never beget'), so the glossary's 'give birth' keeps the birth-in-beauty principle audible.

Accurate unpacking. Plato 210a: 'if the one leading leads rightly', within the lesser/greater mysteries frame Diotima has just set up, and 'these mysteries' refers back to it. It introduces the guide without adding facts.
Fixes the 'every body' / 'everybody' confusion by ear; the meaning is unchanged.

Sound. Plato 211c names the rungs as learnings or subjects of study (μαθήματα), ending in 'that learning which is of beauty itself'. Jowett's own introduction calls the same rungs 'the sciences' and 'a single science of universal beauty' (pg1600.txt lines 341-342). The modern 7.63 already says 'branches of knowledge' and 'the knowledge of beauty everywhere', so the recap now names the rungs the listener has heard, and absolute beauty is no longer 'a mere notion'. No rung is dropped, and 'at last knows what the essence of beauty is' is kept.
Exact. Plato 212a: συνόντος αὐτῷ, 'being together with it'. 'keep company' is within Jowett's 'holding converse with', drops churchy 'communion', and prepares 7.66.
Fine. It echoes 7.65's 'keep company with', so 'that company' is heard as companionship rather than a group. Plato's word here is just 'there' (ἐνταῦθα).
Faithful. Plato 212a: θεοφιλεῖ, 'dear to the gods', which is closer than 'the friend of God'. The plural matches 7.47, and 'if any mortal man can' is kept.

Fine. Plato 212b: 'I myself honor the things of love and practice them above all' (διαφερόντως ἀσκῶ). 'devote myself to his ways' is closer to that than the biblical idiom, and it keeps the first person.

paragraph_problems.issue: Created by R2-112, outside this packet. 7.26 is the agreement that 7.32 recalls, and it still reads 'and of something, too, that a man lacks'. 7.32 now recalls it as 'what one lacks'. That breaks the same-word rule, and 7.26 keeps the 'a man' subject shift that BL2 flagged. Plato 200e has no 'man': 'of those things of which a lack is present to it' (αὐτῷ). Suggest for 7.26: 'First, is love not the love of something — and of something, too, that one lacks?'

Created by R2-131. The conclusion now reads 'So love is also the love of immortality', but its premise two sentences earlier still reads 'love is of the everlasting possession of the good'. 7.55 then recalls it as 'love is of the immortal'. These are the same unidiomatic formula R2-131 removed, and the argument's formula should match at each step. Suggest 7.54: 'love is the love of the everlasting possession of the good' (as 7.52 has it), and 7.55: 'love is the love of the immortal'.

Minor, visible on the page only, outside this packet. R2-113 capitalized Love at 7.38 to match 7.34, but 7.42 ('Then in lacking the beautiful, love also lacks the good?') still lowercases the same subject. Plato 201c has ὁ Ἔρως here. Suggest 'Love also lacks the good'.

summary: SRC3 re-checked all 50 round-2 edits in the 32 paragraphs of chapter 7 against the corrected Jowett (original-en 3521a12d) and pg1600.txt. Where an edit's choice depends on the Greek, I checked it in Burnet's public-domain text (199d-e, 200a, 200e-201c, 203a, 203e, 204d, 205b, 205e, 206b-e, 208a-b, 209a, 211c, 212a). No translation was consulted. The packet's BEFORE and AFTER texts match the work files, and every BEFORE-to-AFTER change maps to a listed edit. I read all 32 AFTER paragraphs in full. Quotes are balanced and reopen correctly across the multi-paragraph speeches; Diotima's speech (7.45-7.66) has no contractions; spelling is American, em dashes are spaced, and there are no ellipses. Every step survives unchanged: love is of something; desire implies lack; Love loves beauty, so lacks beauty and the good; Love is an intermediate spirit; love is of the everlasting possession of the good; birth in beauty; reproduction as mortal immortality; the ladder and its recap. Each reply still fits its question. Result: 48 accept, 2 revise, 0 reject. Revise R2-103: restore 'something' in the father / brother / Love analogy. Revise R2-111: 'fair point' puts 'fair' meaning just into the beauty elenchus, against the glossary. Three follow-ups sit outside the edited spans: 7.26 still says 'a man' where 7.32 now says 'one'; 7.54 and 7.55 keep the 'love is of' formula; 7.42 has lowercase 'love'.
